title: "Panel 1 — Who Covers Whom?"
format: html
---

**Thursday, September 3 · Reading: "Getting Health Insurance" (Book Ch. 1.2)**

This first panel is about how Americans actually get health insurance — the mix of
private coverage (employer plans, the individual market) and public programs
(Medicare, Medicaid, the VHA, TRICARE) that together decide who is covered and who
is not. The reading spans both the private and the public side. We work through the
private side at the board this class and the public side next class, so **read the
whole chapter before the panel** — the discussion reaches into the public programs
before we cover them formally.

Use every question below as a reading guide. On panel day I put a set of these
questions, sometimes reworded, to the drawn panel, and the strongest questions from
the floor tend to come from this list too. You will not know in advance which you
get, so come with the whole thing worked through. Being ready here is what earns
points, whether you are on the panel or asking from the audience.

## Know the landscape

These are answerable straight from the reading. Have specific answers ready.

1. What are the main sources of health insurance in the U.S., and roughly what
   share of the population does each cover?
2. How did employer-sponsored insurance become the dominant source of coverage for
   working-age Americans? What did World War II wage controls and the 1954 tax
   treatment have to do with it?
3. Why is a dollar of employer premium contribution worth more to a worker than a
   dollar of wages spent on the same policy?
4. What is the "non-group" (individual) market, and what did the ACA change about
   how it works — subsidies, guaranteed issue, community rating?
5. Who is eligible for Medicare, and what does each of its four parts (A, B, C, D)
   cover?
6. Who is eligible for Medicaid, and how are its financing and administration
   different from Medicare's?
7. Whom do the Veterans Health Administration and TRICARE cover, and how does the
   VHA differ from every other program in the way it delivers care?
8. For the same service, how can Medicare, Medicaid, and a private insurer each pay
   the provider a different amount?

## Going deeper

No single right answer here. Take a position and be ready to defend it.

1. The U.S. covers people through a patchwork of private and public programs rather
   than one system. What does that fragmentation buy us, and what does it cost us?
2. Employer-sponsored insurance ties your coverage to your job. Whom does that link
   hurt, and how does it shape decisions about changing jobs, starting a business,
   or retiring before 65?
3. The tax exclusion for employer premiums is one of the largest items in the
   federal budget that never comes up for a vote. Who benefits most from it, and is
   it a good use of public money?
4. Medicaid eligibility and benefits vary widely by state. What are the fairness and
   efficiency consequences of a safety-net program whose generosity depends on where
   you live?
5. Medicare covers people over 65 regardless of income, while Medicaid is
   means-tested. Why is public coverage split that way, and would you draw the lines
   differently?
6. More than half of Medicare enrollees now choose a private Medicare Advantage plan
   over traditional Medicare. Why might someone prefer it, and what does the
   government gain or give up by paying private plans to cover them?
7. If you were designing coverage for the country from scratch, would you keep
   employer-based insurance at the center? If not, what would you put in its place?

## Your take

Think about where your own coverage comes from right now — a parent's plan, an
employer, a public program, the marketplace, or nothing at all. What have you
actually noticed about what it does and does not pay for? Name one thing you would
change about how you get covered. Come ready with a concrete example, not just an
opinion.
